title: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations”. Scope: all organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.52

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Trait matching can be tested for many interaction classes, but joining morphology to interaction records is incomplete and causal coevolution is confounded by shared environments. The universal formulation is beyond current coverage.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across documented interactions, test whether organismal structures covary with corresponding competitor, predator, prey or escape-related structures after phylogenetic and environmental controls. Reciprocal functional matching supports the relational claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trait matching does not by itself establish causal shaping.

'Every organism' and 'most essential' are not exhaustively testable.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Interaction archives and trait databases can test visible matching between structures and partners for a biased but real subset of organisms. The universal and 'hidden' wording survives a null result, so discriminating power is low. What existing data can resolve is a proxy: whether known interactions predict form better than environment and phylogeny alone, in guilds that have both traits and links.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Ask what fraction of measured structures are statistically predictable from the traits of competitors, predators, prey, or escape targets, against a phylogeny-and-environment null. A large excess of matched structures would support pervasive relatedness of form; a null match rate would challenge the universal reading only for relations that are visible in the data.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Relations that are 'often hidden' can be postulated whenever a test finds no match, which blocks refutation.

'Every' organism and 'essential' relation have no natural numerical threshold.

Trait matching often restates known natural history (bill and prey size) for a few well-studied guilds.
